questions.q: What does the article say the grand scale of the universe should remind us of?
options: That the earth is the centre of everything
Not quite. The article says: Our own smallness, and the power of the Creator behind it.
Our own smallness, and the power of the Creator behind it
Yes. It is a sign to reflect on, not only a marvel.
That nothing more remains to be discovered
Not quite. The article says: Our own smallness, and the power of the Creator behind it.
That the stars are close to us
Not quite. The article says: Our own smallness, and the power of the Creator behind it.
questions.rationale: “The grand scale of the universe is not just a marvel but also a reminder of human insignificance and the need to acknowledge God’s existence and supremacy.”

questions.q: Which weakness of people does the article point to with the verse “They only know the outward appearance of the life of this world”?
options: A fear of the night sky
Not quite. The article says: Skill in understanding the material world alongside neglect of the greater reality beyond it.
A lack of interest in science
Not quite. The article says: Skill in understanding the material world alongside neglect of the greater reality beyond it.
An inability to learn
Not quite. The article says: Skill in understanding the material world alongside neglect of the greater reality beyond it.
Skill in understanding the material world alongside neglect of the greater reality beyond it
Right. Outward knowledge is not the whole truth.
questions.rationale: “While humans excel in understanding the material world, they often remain ignorant of the greater realities beyond it.”

questions.q: A child kept playing with her doll while a storm shook the ship. What did she say, and what does it picture?
options: “I cannot swim” – the helplessness of man
Not quite. The article says: “My father is the captain; he will not let it sink” – the trust of a believer in God during a crisis.
“Storms always pass” – the value of experience
Not quite. The article says: “My father is the captain; he will not let it sink” – the trust of a believer in God during a crisis.
“My father is the captain; he will not let it sink” – the trust of a believer in God during a crisis
Yes. Such a person lives in hope.
“Let us go home” – the wish to escape
Not quite. The article says: “My father is the captain; he will not let it sink” – the trust of a believer in God during a crisis.
questions.rationale: “In every situation, they can say, ‘God Almighty is the captain of my ship. He’s not going to let it sink.’”

questions.q: What quality, found in man but not in animals, does the article use to explain human discontent?
options: The need for food
Not quite. The article says: The concept of “tomorrow” – man looks to the future for the fulfilment he misses today.
Physical strength
Not quite. The article says: The concept of “tomorrow” – man looks to the future for the fulfilment he misses today.
The concept of “tomorrow” – man looks to the future for the fulfilment he misses today
Well read. Animals live only in the present.
The ability to move
Not quite. The article says: The concept of “tomorrow” – man looks to the future for the fulfilment he misses today.
questions.rationale: “A comparative study of man and animals reveals that the concept of tomorrow is exceptionally found within humans.”

questions.q: Man’s mind has vast potential, yet his lifespan and the earth’s conditions are limited. What does the article conclude?
options: Potential is an illusion
Not quite. The article says: Man needs a far greater world and a longer life for his fulfilment – this life is a training period for the eternal one.
Man should lower his aims
Not quite. The article says: Man needs a far greater world and a longer life for his fulfilment – this life is a training period for the eternal one.
Man needs a far greater world and a longer life for his fulfilment – this life is a training period for the eternal one
Correct. Death is a bridge between the two.
Fulfilment is possible only for a few on earth
Not quite. The article says: Man needs a far greater world and a longer life for his fulfilment – this life is a training period for the eternal one.
questions.rationale: “Realising this reality compels us to believe that humanity requires a vastly greater world and a much longer lifespan for its complete fulfilment.”

questions.article: World Religions and the Spirit of Tolerance
questions.q: How does the article describe the difference between Aryan and Semitic religions in the matter of tolerance?
options: There is no difference of any kind
Not quite. The article says: It is one of philosophy, not practice – one rests it on mutual recognition, the other on mutual respect.
It is one of philosophy, not practice – one rests it on mutual recognition, the other on mutual respect
Yes. Tolerance is the spirit of both.
One limits tolerance to its own followers
Not quite. The article says: It is one of philosophy, not practice – one rests it on mutual recognition, the other on mutual respect.
One teaches tolerance and the other does not
Not quite. The article says: It is one of philosophy, not practice – one rests it on mutual recognition, the other on mutual respect.
questions.rationale: “The basis of tolerance in Aryan religions is on mutual recognition, while its basis in Semitic religions is on mutual respect. This difference is only one of philosophical explanation.”

questions.article: From Hospital Rooms to Heavenly Realms
questions.q: Watching a great modern hospital at work, what kind of “empire” did the writer feel is still waiting to be built?
options: A trading empire
Not quite. The article says: A spiritual one – of hearts, built through love, reason and wisdom, not force.
A spiritual one – of hearts, built through love, reason and wisdom, not force
Right. Not of territories.
A political empire
Not quite. The article says: A spiritual one – of hearts, built through love, reason and wisdom, not force.
A larger medical empire
Not quite. The article says: A spiritual one – of hearts, built through love, reason and wisdom, not force.
questions.rationale: “The real call is to build an empire of hearts, not territories. One that invites people to understand God’s creation plan, not through fear or force, but through love, reason, and wisdom.”

questions.q: To what does the article compare the Earth, and what does it say man has done?
options: A desert – which man has made green
Not quite. The article says: A mother’s womb that provides everything needed – which man has damaged through greed and carelessness.
A ship – which man has steered well
Not quite. The article says: A mother’s womb that provides everything needed – which man has damaged through greed and carelessness.
A mother’s womb that provides everything needed – which man has damaged through greed and carelessness
Yes. It also calls us to prepare for the Hereafter.
A marketplace – which man has improved
Not quite. The article says: A mother’s womb that provides everything needed – which man has damaged through greed and carelessness.
questions.rationale: “Earth… a haven as vital to us as a mother’s womb is to her child… human greed and carelessness have severely damaged this planet.”

questions.q: What does the article call the secret of success, for a person or a nation?
options: Learning to live with problems and building one’s life in spite of them
Exactly. A problem-free life is not on offer.
Exchanging old problems for new ones
Not quite. The article says: Learning to live with problems and building one’s life in spite of them.
Waiting for problems to end
Not quite. The article says: Learning to live with problems and building one’s life in spite of them.
Removing every problem first
Not quite. The article says: Learning to live with problems and building one’s life in spite of them.
questions.rationale: “The only secret of success for both the individual and the nation is to learn to live with their problems and construct their lives despite their existence.”

questions.q: The writer’s slippers were stolen on a train and he walked home barefoot. What did the experience teach him?
options: That one should never sleep on a journey
Not quite. The article says: Even the smallest things are blessings from God, whose worth we notice only when they are gone.
That trains are unsafe
Not quite. The article says: Even the smallest things are blessings from God, whose worth we notice only when they are gone.
Even the smallest things are blessings from God, whose worth we notice only when they are gone
Well read. A moment to say Alhamdulillah.
That slippers should be cheap
Not quite. The article says: Even the smallest things are blessings from God, whose worth we notice only when they are gone.
questions.rationale: “We are surrounded by blessings—big and small, visible and hidden. But most of the time, we only realize their worth when they’re gone.”
